title: Kinship, Crime, and the Clan Debate in Germany
summary: Maya and Daniel unpack a landmark report from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime examining Arabic-speaking criminal networks in Germany. They explore the roots of long-established Mardin-origin clans, the rise of newer Syrian networks, and what law enforcement often gets wrong about kinship and organized crime.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: If you follow European security, organized crime, or immigration politics, you know that few topics spark fiercer debate in Germany right now than so-called clan crime. It dominates headlines, political campaigns, and television dramas. But behind the sensationalism, the actual mechanics of these networks are often misunderstood.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right, and that brings us to the report we're breaking down today. It's titled Kinship and Crime: Arabic-Speaking Criminal Networks in Germany, authored by Dr Mahmoud Jaraba and published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. Anyone working in policing, intelligence, policymaking, or civil rights is going to want to pay close attention to this, because it challenges a lot of lazy assumptions.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. Dr Jaraba draws on over a decade of ethnographic fieldwork conducted between 2015 and 2026, combining confidential interviews with extended family members, law enforcement, and social workers, alongside online ethnography and investigation files. His central premise is simple: differentiation is not minimization. In other words, understanding the exact social structures of these groups is the only way to craft effective, rights-based interventions without stigmatizing entire communities.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That's a crucial distinction. The report makes it very clear that kinship or an Arabic surname shouldn't be treated as criminal evidence. Jaraba focuses on two distinct, overlapping fields: the long-established Mardin-origin clans and newer Syrian formations that arrived after 2015. Where does the story start historically?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It starts in south-eastern Türkiye, specifically Mardin Province, and often a single village called al-Rashidiya, or Üçkavak in Turkish. Following the founding of the Turkish Republic in 1923, many families in this region faced marginalization and language repression. Between the 1920s and 1960s, a wave migrated into Syria and Lebanon, where they often lacked legal status and access to public services. Then, when the Lebanese Civil War erupted in 1975, many fled to Europe, particularly Germany.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And when they arrived in Germany, their legal standing was precarious, to put it mildly.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Very precarious. Many were placed under Duldung, or tolerated stay. That meant a suspension of deportation with severe restrictions on work, travel, and education. The report notes community estimates that between ten and thirty percent, even into the second and third generations, still live under those conditions today. In the early 1980s, when lawful avenues were blocked, some men turned to petty theft, untaxed cigarettes, counterfeit goods, and street drug dealing to support families and send remittances back to Mardin or Beirut.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Then comes 1989. The Berlin Wall falls.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. The opening of borders and a surge in nightlife and drug demand created massive new illicit opportunities. One interviewee recounted how young people flooded Berlin for freedom and drugs, creating a demand that existing criminal elements rushed to fill. Through the 1990s and 2000s, these activities institutionalized within smaller kin units called buyut, the extended family lineages nested inside the wider ashira.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Help us understand those terms, because the report spends time dissecting them. What is the ashira, and how does it relate to the buyut?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: An ashira is a patrilineal kin formation that organizes social life, mediation, protection, and access to resources. Several asha'ir might form a broader tribal confederation, a qabila. Within the clan, you have the buyut, the extended family households. Jaraba emphasizes that the ashira is not a criminal cartel; it's a social framework. But within certain buyut, family loyalty and trust were instrumentalized to run criminal ventures. One insider quoted in the report said, <short pause> loyalty was the currency: first your brothers, then your cousins, and only after that outsiders, because one weak link brings the police to the entire house.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And that network provided bases across Germany, right? Beyond Berlin, into North Rhine-Westphalia, Bremen, and Lower Saxony.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. Relatives could provide logistics, safe houses, and local backing. Over decades, some of these segments gained notorious public visibility through high-profile crimes. Think of the 2017 theft of the Big Maple Leaf, the massive hundred-kilogram gold coin stolen from Berlin's Bode Museum, or the 2019 Green Vault burglary in Dresden. Prosecutors linked suspects to members of the Berlin-based Remmo family.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Those cases cemented the public image of the clans. But what's happening now with the younger generation born in Germany? Are they just copying their parents?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: No, and this is one of Jaraba's key findings. The generational dynamic has shifted significantly. For the younger cohort, born and raised in Germany, traditional patriarchal authority and old concepts of honour or social shame, like ayb, have weakened. Instead, you see an entrepreneurial turn. They're engaging in transactional, cross-ethnic networks, blending online logistics with offline operations. Rather than big, public shows of force, many focus on co-opting insiders, exploiting administrative blind spots, and gathering intelligence on police tactics.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: The Bode Museum case is actually a prime example of that inside-access dynamic, wasn't it? Working with a museum security guard who was a childhood friend.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Precisely. Now, let's contrast that with the Syrian formations, which represent an entirely different chapter.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right. Until the mid-2010s, the Syrian diaspora in Germany was relatively small and not connected to organized crime debates. But the Syrian civil war changed everything.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Radically. Destatis recorded about 1.281 million people with Syrian migration history living in Germany by 2025. Many arrived as extended family networks from rural regions where tribal authority was often stronger than state institutions. There was another significant uptick in arrivals starting around 2021; in 2023 alone, Germany registered over 102,000 Syrian arrivals, driven by worsening conditions in Syria and host countries.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: How do police assess Syrian involvement in crime? Is it fair to speak of Syrian clans in the same breath as the Mardin-origin families?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The report warns against that. Assessments from state police bodies, like the North Rhine-Westphalia LKA and the Euphrat project by regional police cooperation bodies, remain cautious. They found that organized crime and clan crime among Syrian suspects had only been confirmed in individual cases, even while noting an increase in violent street crime among young people. What we are seeing is not a fully consolidated clan mafia across the Syrian community, but rather loose youth formations, regional networks, and specialized smuggling rings.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's dig into those specialized networks, because the report details a couple of striking legal cases.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes. One major example is the Al-Sarawi smuggling network. In November 2025, the Traunstein Regional Court in Bavaria convicted four defendants associated with this group. The court established that this network organized a significant share of commercial migrant smuggling along the Balkan route, using life-endangering methods that in one instance resulted in death. The proceedings also uncovered attempted honour murder, extortionate kidnapping, and severe bodily harm.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And there was another case involving genuine German residency documents, wasn't there?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: In April 2026, the Federal Police ran a large-scale raid targeting around 50 Syrian nationals suspected of mailing their genuine German residence permits back to Syria so lookalikes could enter Germany or the Schengen area. The Clan Task Force of the Saxony State Criminal Police Office investigated possible clan connections. It shows how everyday social resources and trust are repurposed for illicit logistics.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: If we look at geography, how do the Mardin-origin groups and Syrian groups compare across Germany and Europe?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That's a major divergence. Mardin-origin clans are estimated at 35,000 to 50,000 people, heavily clustered in specific cities: Berlin, parts of North Rhine-Westphalia like Essen and Duisburg, Bremen, and Lower Saxony. In Europe, they have dense hubs in Sweden, Denmark, and the Netherlands. Syrian communities, by contrast, are far more dispersed across Germany, in Berlin, Hamburg, Essen, Dortmund, Leipzig, Halle, Munich, and smaller towns. Across Europe, their networks are multi-node and mobile, kept tightly coordinated through digital channels like Telegram and TikTok, alongside physical spaces like madafa, the traditional clan salons or guesthouses.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's talk about financing and value transfer, because that's where hawala enters the picture.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Hawala is critical here. It's an informal value-transfer system based on trusted intermediaries, completely outside the formal banking system. If someone in Berlin wants to send 400 euros to a relative in Deir ez-Zor, they give the cash to a local broker, get a code, message it to the relative, and the counterpart broker in Deir ez-Zor pays out the cash. Later, the brokers settle up through trade or couriers. Hawala isn't inherently criminal; millions rely on it for remittances. But organized networks exploit that exact same trust-based speed and opacity to launder money and fund smuggling.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And because it runs on shared hometowns, dialects, or family names, trust is virtually instantaneous. Speaking of dispute resolution outside the legal system, the report gives a fascinating account of informal mediation, or sulha.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, in German media these mediators are often dubbed Friedensrichter, or peace judges, though that's an outside label, not their own. When serious violence breaks out, informal mediation steps in to avoid state courts or bloody feuds. The report details an extraordinary case between Clan Omeirat and Clan Fakro, both originally from al-Rashidiya.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Walk us through that timeline, because it really illustrates the transnational scale of these ties.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It began in December 2020, when Saleh Omeirat was killed in Sweden after a drug-related financial dispute. Clan Omeirat blamed Ahmad Fakro, who fled to Lebanon. In January 2022, Ahmad Fakro was murdered in Beirut. Then, in April 2022, Saleh's father, Idris Omeirat, travelled from Germany back to their ancestral village of al-Rashidiya in Türkiye for a funeral. Clan Fakro members killed him there. That very same day, Clan Omeirat retaliated by killing Mohamad Fakro in the village.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Four killings across Sweden, Lebanon, and Türkiye, tied directly back to families living across Germany.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. To prevent an all-out war, clan elders from Germany, Sweden, Lebanon, and Türkiye held regular cross-border meetings. Finally, in September 2024, they reached a formal sulha in the village, agreeing that two deaths on each side balanced the ledger, and committed both sides to end retaliation.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That's an incredible look at how alternative normative orders operate across international borders. The report also highlights transnational fraud networks operating from Türkiye targeting German citizens.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right, the false police officer call-centre scams. Callers in Türkiye pose as German police officers, manipulating elderly German victims into handing over cash, gold, and valuables to local runners under the guise of keeping their assets safe. The report profiles two specific cases: Halit D, known online as Papa Kralle, and Heisem M.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What happened with Halit D?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: After being deported from Germany to Türkiye, Halit D and his brothers allegedly ran an İzmir-based call-centre operation. In December 2020, Turkish police raided premises in İzmir with German cooperation, seizing millions in assets. In September 2022, a Turkish court sentenced defendants in the ring, naming Halit D as an alleged manager. However, an appeals court set aside that verdict, releasing him pending retrial. He went right back onto social media, flaunting luxury lifestyles and denying all charges.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And Heisem M?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: His case is just as striking. German authorities linked him to the January 2009 killing of Hussein El-Zein and the shooting of his fiancée near Bremen, after which he fled to Türkiye. Years later, he surfaced in Mersin, accused by Turkish authorities of running a call-centre scam that defrauded German pensioners of nearly 1.6 million euros across simultaneous raids in six Turkish provinces. He also denied the charges during ongoing court proceedings. These cases show how actors exploit cross-border family networks and safe havens when facing legal pressure in Germany.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Then there's the street level, which has gotten intense media coverage lately in Germany: youth gangs like Jamaat Talahon and Ajyan al-Bahnof.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right, Jamaat Talahon, meaning the come-here crew, and Ajyan al-Bahnof, the railway-station boys. These groups of teenagers and young men, mostly aged 14 to 25, gather around transit hubs and shopping areas in Berlin, Hamburg, Essen, Stuttgart, and Nuremberg. They engage in shoplifting, low-level drug dealing, street brawls, and use TikTok and Instagram to project tough reputations. Interestingly, while some come from Syrian or Mardin backgrounds, they often operate outside traditional family oversight. Some are multi-ethnic, fluid groups driven more by street culture and viral trends than clan allegiance.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which brings us to the policy debate. How has the German state responded, and where does Dr Jaraba see flaws in that approach?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Starting around 2018, state police in North Rhine-Westphalia, Berlin, Lower Saxony, and Bremen formalized clan crime reporting, and the BKA added it to national reporting in 2020. But the term remains heavily contested. Critics and experts point out that relying on lists of family names risks racial profiling and guilt by association. A law-abiding person who shares a surname with a known offender ends up carrying a collective stigma.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So what does the report recommend? How should authorities tackle these illicit networks without repeating past mistakes?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The recommendations are very concrete. First: target identifiable criminal actors and markets, not surnames or ethnic groups. Kinship shouldn't be treated as criminal evidence.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Second, intervene early in developing structures. Don't wait for Syrian networks to institutionalize like the older networks did.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. Disrupting networks after multi-generational reputations and money-laundering channels have set in is infinitely harder. Third, follow the money and target criminal brokers. Street-level arrests don't stop the crime if the financial infrastructure, real estate, cash-intensive businesses, and hawala nodes remain intact. Investigators need early asset recovery and should focus on the brokers who supply fake documents, arrange transport, or move funds.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the report also touches on immigration law, specifically post-Assad Syria.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, carefully. With the fall of the Assad regime changing the context in Syria, the report notes that deportation of serious or persistent non-citizen offenders could be part of a disruption strategy, provided removal is lawful, safe, and strictly adheres to the principle of non-refoulement under international law. But it emphasizes this should strictly target serious convicted offenders, not Syrian refugees broadly.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: What about the social and community side? Policing alone obviously can't solve this.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That's a huge point. Jaraba stresses youth prevention: sustained funding for social workers, schools, and neighbourhood programmes to prevent marginalized youth from slipping into street gangs. And engaging credible community partners. Many family members detest the violence and criminal stigma. Informal mediation can help de-escalate feuds, though Jaraba warns it must never supersede the formal criminal justice system or silence victims.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It's a nuanced, rigorous roadmap that strips away political hyperbole and replaces it with empirical reality.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Absolutely. Looking ahead, this report is the foundation for two upcoming studies from the Global Initiative: one focusing specifically on migrant smuggling corridors and another on transnational drug markets involving these exact networks.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: We'll definitely be watching for those. If you want to read the full report, check out Kinship and Crime: Arabic-Speaking Criminal Networks in Germany by Dr Mahmoud Jaraba on the GI-TOC website. Maya, thanks for walking us through it.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Always a pleasure, Daniel. Thanks for listening, everyone.
